concepts.title: Why cache, and the hit-ratio arithmetic
concepts.summary: A cache trades memory for latency and origin load. Average latency is hit ratio times cache time plus miss ratio times origin time, and origin load is traffic times miss ratio. Going from 95 to 99 percent hits cuts origin load five-fold.
concepts.production: A catalogue API at 5,000 requests a second sent 250 a second to the database at 95 percent hits and only 50 at 99 percent.
concepts.interview: Do this arithmetic aloud. The five-fold insight impresses interviewers.

concepts.title: How Redis executes commands
concepts.summary: Redis runs commands on one main thread (newer versions add I/O threading), so every command is atomic but one slow command delays everyone. Keep commands O(1) or O(log N), and avoid huge keys and full scans.
concepts.production: A {{KEYS *}} on a production cache froze every client for seconds.
concepts.interview: Explain why atomicity comes free but latency is shared.

concepts.title: A cache is not the source of truth
concepts.summary: Design so losing the entire cache only makes things slower. Replication and persistence are best effort for a cache. Data that cannot be rebuilt from elsewhere belongs in a database.
concepts.production: After a failover wiped sessions stored only in Redis, users were logged out and carts vanished.
concepts.interview: Always answer: what happens when Redis is empty?

concepts.title: Redis, Valkey and managed services
concepts.summary: Redis 8 is offered under a choice of licences that includes AGPLv3. Valkey is the BSD-licensed Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2 and is supported by major cloud providers. Core caching commands are compatible, while newer modules and features diverge, so check what you depend on.
concepts.production: A team moving to Valkey found a module command they relied on was not available and had to change the design.
concepts.interview: Know the licensing story and that managed services such as ElastiCache may offer both engines.

concepts.title: Data structures at a glance
concepts.summary: Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps and HyperLogLog are classic. Redis 8 also bundles JSON, time series, probabilistic structures and vector sets. Choose the structure that matches your access pattern, not just strings.
concepts.production: Storing a user as a hash let the app read one field without parsing a whole JSON string.
concepts.interview: Match a structure to three problems: leaderboard, unique count, queue.

concepts.title: What belongs in a cache
concepts.summary: Cache data that is read often, costly to compute, tolerant of slight staleness and easy to key. Avoid highly personalised results, rarely repeated queries and data that must always be fresh.
concepts.production: Per-user search results had a 3 percent hit ratio and only added cost, so they were removed from the cache.
concepts.interview: Name two things you would deliberately not cache.

concepts.title: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
concepts.summary: The application checks the cache, on a miss reads the database, then stores the result with a TTL. On writes it updates the database and deletes the key. It is the default pattern because the cache can fail without breaking correctness.
concepts.production: A product API used cache-aside with a 10 minute TTL and survived a Redis restart with only a latency bump.
concepts.interview: Describe the read path and the write path, and why you delete rather than update.

concepts.title: Read-through
concepts.summary: The cache layer itself loads missing data from the database through a loader function, so callers only talk to the cache. Redis does not do this by itself; you get it from a library, a data-integration product or a wrapper you write.
concepts.production: A shared caching library gave every service the same loader and TTL behaviour instead of ad hoc code.
concepts.interview: Contrast with cache-aside: who owns the loading logic?

concepts.title: Write-through
concepts.summary: Every write goes to the cache and synchronously to the database before returning. Reads are always warm and consistent, at the cost of slower writes and caching data that may never be read.
concepts.production: A reference-data service used write-through so lookups never saw stale values after an admin edit.
concepts.interview: State the cost: write latency and wasted memory for cold data.

concepts.title: Write-behind (write-back)
concepts.summary: Writes land in the cache and are flushed to the database asynchronously in batches. Writes are very fast, but a crash before the flush loses data and ordering is harder. Use a durable queue or stream, not memory alone.
concepts.production: A counters service batched page-view writes every few seconds and cut database writes by 95 percent, accepting a small loss window.
concepts.interview: Say clearly what you can lose and how you would limit it.

concepts.title: Write-around
concepts.summary: Writes go straight to the database and bypass the cache. Reads still use cache-aside. It avoids filling the cache with data that is written often but read rarely, at the price of a miss on the first read.
concepts.production: Audit logs were written around the cache because they were almost never read back.
concepts.interview: Give an example of write-heavy, read-light data.

concepts.title: Refresh-ahead and stale-while-revalidate
concepts.summary: Refresh hot entries before they expire, or serve a slightly stale value while one request refreshes it in the background. Users never wait for a reload and stampedes are avoided, at the cost of extra complexity and some staleness.
concepts.production: A pricing page served a value up to 30 seconds old while a single background call refreshed it.
concepts.interview: Explain soft versus hard TTL.

concepts.title: Negative caching
concepts.summary: Cache "not found" results for a short TTL so repeated lookups for missing ids do not hit the database. Combine with validation or a Bloom filter to blunt cache penetration attacks.
concepts.production: Bots requesting random ids hammered the database until misses were cached for 60 seconds.
concepts.interview: Say how long you cache a miss and why it must be short.

concepts.title: Multi-level caches: in-process plus Redis
concepts.summary: A small in-process cache (L1) absorbs the hottest reads with zero network cost, and Redis (L2) is shared. You must handle invalidation across instances, usually with short L1 TTLs or pub/sub invalidation messages.
concepts.production: An in-process cache with a 5 second TTL removed a hot key that was saturating one Redis shard.
concepts.interview: Describe how L1 copies on many pods stay reasonably fresh.

concepts.title: Client-side caching with RESP3 tracking
concepts.summary: Redis can track which keys a client has cached locally and send invalidation messages when they change (RESP3 client tracking). node-redis v5 adds support. It gives near-zero latency reads with server-driven invalidation, at the cost of client memory and complexity.
concepts.production: A read-heavy configuration service served from process memory and was invalidated by the server on change.
concepts.interview: Say what the server remembers and the memory trade-off.

concepts.title: Choosing TTLs
concepts.summary: A TTL is a staleness budget. Pick it from how wrong the data may be and for how long, not from habit. Longer TTLs raise hit ratio and lower freshness. Always set a TTL on cache keys so abandoned entries cannot live forever.
concepts.production: Product descriptions used 1 hour and stock levels 5 seconds, because users tolerate stale text but not stale stock.
concepts.interview: Justify one TTL by the business tolerance for stale data.

concepts.title: TTL jitter
concepts.summary: Add random variation (for example plus or minus 10 to 20 percent) so keys created together do not expire together. Without jitter, a bulk load produces a synchronised wave of misses.
concepts.production: A nightly warm-up wrote 200,000 keys with a 1 hour TTL and caused an hourly database spike until jitter was added.
concepts.interview: Show the one-line formula for jittered TTL.
concepts.code: const ttl = Math.round(base * (0.9 + Math.random() * 0.2)); // base plus or minus 10 percent

concepts.title: maxmemory and eviction policies
concepts.summary: When memory is full Redis applies {{maxmemory-policy}}. {{noeviction}} rejects writes, {{allkeys-lru}} and {{allkeys-lfu}} evict from all keys, {{volatile-*}} policies only evict keys with a TTL, and {{volatile-ttl}} evicts the soonest to expire. For a pure cache, {{allkeys-lru}} or {{allkeys-lfu}} is typical.
concepts.production: A cache left on {{noeviction}} started returning OOM errors to the application when it filled up.
concepts.interview: Say which policy you choose for a cache versus a session store and why.

concepts.title: LRU versus LFU, and approximation
concepts.summary: LRU evicts what was used least recently; LFU evicts what is used least often and resists one-off scans that would flush a popular key. Redis approximates both by sampling a few keys instead of tracking exact order, which is cheaper and nearly as good.
concepts.production: Switching to LFU kept a popular catalogue warm while a crawler walked millions of one-off URLs.
concepts.interview: Explain why sampling is acceptable and what a scan does to LRU.

concepts.title: Lazy and active expiry
concepts.summary: Expired keys are removed when accessed (lazy) and by a background process that samples keys with TTLs (active). Expired keys can briefly occupy memory, and a burst of expirations can add CPU work.
concepts.production: A mass expiry of millions of keys at once produced a short latency bump on the primary.
concepts.interview: Describe why memory does not drop at the exact TTL.

concepts.title: Per-field expiry in hashes
concepts.summary: Recent Redis and Valkey versions can set expiry on individual hash fields, so one hash can hold many short-lived entries. Check your engine version before depending on it.
concepts.production: A per-user hash held feature-flag overrides that each expired after different durations.
concepts.interview: Mention it as the answer to "how do I expire part of a hash?".

concepts.title: Memory pressure and hit ratio
concepts.summary: Evictions lower the hit ratio and send load to the database, which raises latency and can start a feedback loop. Watch {{evicted_keys}} and {{used_memory}} and size the cache so the hot working set fits.
concepts.production: A deploy increased value sizes, evictions rose, hit ratio fell and the database overloaded.
concepts.interview: Say which two metrics warn you that the cache is too small.

concepts.title: TTL-only versus explicit invalidation
concepts.summary: TTL-only is simple but allows staleness up to the TTL. Explicit invalidation deletes or refreshes keys when data changes, giving fresher reads but needing every write path to cooperate. Most systems combine both: events for freshness, TTL as a safety net.
concepts.production: Missing one admin write path left stale data around until the TTL finally expired.
concepts.interview: Say why a TTL is still needed even with event invalidation.

concepts.title: Delete the key rather than update it
concepts.summary: After a database write, delete the cache entry and let the next read repopulate it. Updating the cache directly means two writers racing to set the value and a higher chance of storing something stale.
concepts.production: Two concurrent updates wrote different values to the cache in the opposite order of the database commits.
concepts.interview: Explain the race that deleting avoids.

concepts.title: The cache-aside race
concepts.summary: A reader misses, loads the old row, a writer updates the database and deletes the key, then the reader stores its old value. The cache is stale until the TTL. Mitigate with short TTLs, versioned values, delayed double delete or leases.
concepts.production: Users saw an old price for minutes after an update, because a slow reader repopulated the cache after the delete.
concepts.interview: Walk through the interleaving on a whiteboard.

concepts.title: Event-driven invalidation
concepts.summary: Publish change events from the source of truth (outbox, change data capture or application events) and have consumers delete or refresh keys. Plain pub/sub can drop messages if a subscriber is down, so use a durable stream for important invalidations.
concepts.production: A CDC pipeline invalidated product keys within a second of a database update, regardless of which service wrote it.
concepts.interview: Say what happens if an invalidation message is lost.

concepts.title: Versioned keys and namespaces
concepts.summary: Include a version in the key, such as {{catalog:v7:item:42}}, and bump the version to invalidate a whole group at once. Old keys simply age out through TTL or eviction.
concepts.production: Releasing a new serialisation format bumped a version prefix so no code ever read old-format values.
concepts.interview: Contrast with deleting thousands of keys by pattern.

concepts.title: Tag-based and dependency invalidation
concepts.summary: Record which cache keys depend on an entity (for example a set of keys per product id) and delete that set when the entity changes. It gives precise invalidation for composite cached views but costs memory and writes.
concepts.production: A category page cached 20 products and was invalidated whenever any of them changed.
concepts.interview: Compare with short TTLs for composite objects.

concepts.title: Cache stampede (dogpile)
concepts.summary: When a popular key expires, many requests miss at once and all rebuild it, overloading the origin. Defend with single-flight or a lock so one request rebuilds, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate and probabilistic early refresh.
concepts.production: A trending article expired and 800 concurrent requests ran the same expensive query.
concepts.interview: Name three defences and which you would use first.

concepts.title: Cache avalanche
concepts.summary: Many keys expire together, or the cache goes down, and the whole load lands on the database. Spread expiry with jitter, run Redis highly available, add circuit breakers and keep database capacity for a cold cache.
concepts.production: A restart emptied the cache at peak traffic and took the database down for ten minutes.
concepts.interview: Explain how you would restart a cache safely at peak.

concepts.title: Cache penetration
concepts.summary: Requests for keys that never exist always miss and always reach the database, whether by bug or attack. Use negative caching, input validation, rate limits and a Bloom filter in front for large id spaces.
concepts.production: Scrapers requested random product ids and generated database load with a 0 percent hit ratio.
concepts.interview: Say how you would protect the database from nonexistent ids.

concepts.title: Hot keys
concepts.summary: One key getting a huge share of traffic saturates a single shard or the single main thread. Remedies: an in-process L1 cache, replicating the value under several suffixed keys, read replicas, or splitting counters across keys and summing.
concepts.production: A viral post's key took most of one cluster node's CPU until reads were served from local memory.
concepts.interview: Say how you detect a hot key.

concepts.title: Big keys
concepts.summary: Huge strings, hashes or lists make reads and deletes slow, block the main thread and cause latency spikes and uneven memory. Split into smaller keys, page large collections and use {{UNLINK}} to delete asynchronously.
concepts.production: Deleting a 2 GB list with {{DEL}} blocked Redis for seconds.
concepts.interview: Know why {{UNLINK}} exists.

concepts.title: Cache poisoning and key collisions
concepts.summary: If keys omit a dimension that changes the response (user, tenant, locale, API version), one user can receive another's data. Build keys from every input that affects the result, and never cache responses containing per-user data under shared keys.
concepts.production: A localised page was cached without the locale in its key and showed German text to English users.
concepts.interview: Give a checklist of dimensions a key must include.

concepts.title: Cold starts and warm-up
concepts.summary: A new or flushed cache has no hot data, so traffic hits the origin. Pre-warm the hottest keys, ramp traffic gradually, and keep the origin able to survive a short period of low hit ratio.
concepts.production: A blue-green cache swap sent all traffic to an empty cache until a warm-up job was added.
concepts.interview: Describe a safe cache migration.

concepts.title: Stale reads from ordering and replicas
concepts.summary: Replication is asynchronous, so reading from a replica can return old values or miss a just-written key. Concurrent writers can also overwrite newer values with older ones. Use versions or timestamps and read from the primary when freshness is essential.
concepts.production: A user saved a profile and the next page load, served from a replica, showed the old one.
concepts.interview: Say when you accept replica reads and when you do not.

concepts.title: Key naming and namespaces
concepts.summary: Use a consistent, readable scheme such as {{service:entity:id:variant}}. Include a version where formats change, keep keys short but meaningful, and never build keys from unvalidated user input.
concepts.production: A clear prefix let operators list and measure the memory of one feature's keys.
concepts.interview: Show your key format for a user profile and a list page.

concepts.title: Strings, hashes and JSON
concepts.summary: Strings suit opaque blobs and counters. Hashes store fields you read or update independently and are memory-efficient for small objects. The JSON type supports path queries on documents in Redis 8 and Redis Stack. Pick one by how you read and update.
concepts.production: Switching a 40-field object from a JSON string to a hash cut read bandwidth for the common two-field read.
concepts.interview: Say when a whole-object string beats a hash.

concepts.title: Serialisation and compression
concepts.summary: JSON is simple and debuggable; MessagePack or Protobuf are smaller and faster. Compress only large values, because compression costs CPU and small values rarely benefit. Remember {{Date}}, {{BigInt}} and {{undefined}} do not round-trip through JSON.
concepts.production: Compressing 50 KB responses cut memory by 70 percent while 200 byte values were left alone.
concepts.interview: Name a type that does not survive {{JSON.stringify}}.

concepts.title: Sorted sets for leaderboards and windows
concepts.summary: A sorted set keeps members ordered by score with O(log N) updates and rank queries. Use it for leaderboards, top-N, time-ordered indexes and sliding-window rate limiters.
concepts.production: A game leaderboard used {{ZADD}} and {{ZREVRANGE}} for the top 100 in under a millisecond.
concepts.interview: State the complexity of adding and of fetching a range.

concepts.title: Counting with sets, HyperLogLog and bitmaps
concepts.summary: Sets count exact uniques at a memory cost; HyperLogLog gives approximate unique counts in about 12 KB regardless of cardinality; bitmaps track boolean flags per integer id very compactly.
concepts.production: Daily unique visitors used HyperLogLog and cost kilobytes instead of gigabytes.
concepts.interview: Say what error HyperLogLog trades for memory (around 1 percent).

concepts.title: Memory overhead per key
concepts.summary: Every key has overhead beyond its value (metadata, expiry, allocator rounding). Millions of tiny keys can cost more than their data. Pack small related values into hashes and measure with {{MEMORY USAGE}} instead of guessing.
concepts.production: 10 million tiny string keys used far more memory than the same data grouped into bucketed hashes.
concepts.interview: Explain why many small keys can be wasteful.

concepts.title: Batch reads: MGET and pipelining
concepts.summary: Round trips dominate latency. Fetch many keys with {{MGET}}, or send commands together in a pipeline so one network wait serves many. In Cluster, keys must be grouped by slot.
concepts.production: Loading 50 list items one by one took 50 round trips; one pipeline took one.
concepts.interview: Describe the difference between pipelining and a transaction.

concepts.title: Rate limiting
concepts.summary: A fixed window uses {{INCR}} with {{EXPIRE}}; sliding windows use sorted sets; token buckets use a Lua script for atomic refill and spend. Redis gives one shared counter across all app instances.
concepts.production: An API gateway enforced per-key limits across 30 pods with a single Redis script.
concepts.interview: Explain why in-memory limiters fail behind multiple instances.

concepts.title: Distributed locks
concepts.summary: A lock uses {{SET key token NX PX ttl}} and release only if the token matches (a Lua compare-and-delete). Locks expire, so a slow holder can lose it; use fencing tokens for correctness-critical work and treat Redis locks as efficiency tools, not guarantees.
concepts.production: Two workers ran a billing job at once after a GC pause outlived the lock TTL.
concepts.interview: State the limits of Redis locks and mention fencing.

concepts.title: Session storage
concepts.summary: Sessions fit Redis well: fast reads, TTL for idle expiry, and shared across instances. Persist and replicate if a lost session is costly, and keep the session small.
concepts.production: Moving sessions out of process memory let rolling deploys happen without logging anyone out.
concepts.interview: Say what persistence you need for sessions versus a pure cache.

concepts.title: Job queues and streams
concepts.summary: Lists support simple queues; BullMQ builds reliable queues with retries, delays and rate limits on Redis; Streams provide an append-only log with consumer groups and acknowledgements. Plan for persistence, because queued work is not rebuildable.
concepts.production: Using the cache instance for a job queue meant an eviction policy silently dropped jobs.
concepts.interview: Explain why queues and caches should not share eviction settings.

concepts.title: Pub/sub limitations
concepts.summary: Classic pub/sub is fire and forget: subscribers that are down miss messages, and there is no replay. Use Streams when you need durability or consumer groups.
concepts.production: Cache invalidation messages were lost during a pod restart until a stream replaced pub/sub.
concepts.interview: Say when pub/sub is acceptable.

concepts.title: Idempotency keys and deduplication
concepts.summary: Store processed ids or request keys with {{SET NX}} and a TTL so retries do not repeat side effects. Keep the TTL longer than the longest retry window.
concepts.production: A payment endpoint used a Redis key per client request id to stop double charges, backed by a database constraint.
concepts.interview: Say why Redis alone is not enough for money.

concepts.title: Replication and replica lag
concepts.summary: Replicas copy the primary asynchronously, so they can lag and a failover can lose recent writes. Use replicas to scale reads of tolerant data and for availability, not for strong consistency.
concepts.production: Reads from replicas after a write occasionally returned the old value for a few milliseconds.
concepts.interview: Describe what asynchronous replication means for failover.

concepts.title: Sentinel versus Cluster
concepts.summary: Sentinel monitors a primary and replicas and promotes a replica on failure, but all data fits one primary. Cluster shards data across many primaries by hash slot and also provides failover. Managed services often hide the details.
concepts.production: A dataset outgrew one machine, so the team moved from Sentinel to Cluster.
concepts.interview: Pick one for a 500 GB working set and justify.

concepts.title: Hash slots and hash tags
concepts.summary: Cluster divides keys into 16,384 slots using CRC16 of the key. A hash tag, the part in braces such as {{{user:1}:cart}}, forces related keys into the same slot so multi-key commands work.
concepts.production: Cart and profile keys shared a tag so a transaction could touch both.
concepts.interview: Compute or explain how a key maps to a slot. The slot lab below does it for you.

concepts.title: Multi-key operations in Cluster
concepts.summary: Commands touching several keys (MGET, transactions, Lua scripts) require all keys in one slot, otherwise they fail with a cross-slot error. Design key tags up front and avoid cross-entity transactions.
concepts.production: A script reading two users' keys failed with CROSSSLOT in production because no tag tied them together.
concepts.interview: Say how you would restructure keys to allow a multi-key script.

concepts.title: Persistence: RDB and AOF
concepts.summary: RDB takes point-in-time snapshots; AOF logs every write and can fsync each second. Persistence helps a cache restart warm and is essential for non-rebuildable data, but forking for a snapshot can add latency.
concepts.production: A cache with RDB restarted with its hot data instead of empty, avoiding a stampede.
concepts.interview: Compare the data-loss window of RDB and AOF.

concepts.title: Failover and the data-loss window
concepts.summary: During failover, writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated are lost, and clients briefly cannot write. Make clients retry with timeouts, and avoid storing irreplaceable data without understanding this window.
concepts.production: A failover dropped a few seconds of counters; the business accepted it because the counts were approximate.
concepts.interview: State the guarantee Redis gives and does not give.

concepts.title: Resharding and capacity growth
concepts.summary: Adding shards moves slots between nodes, which temporarily costs CPU and network. Plan headroom, add nodes before saturation and test resharding under load.
concepts.production: Resharding at peak traffic raised latency until it was rescheduled to a quiet window.
concepts.interview: Describe how you would grow a cluster safely.

concepts.title: Choosing a client: node-redis or ioredis
concepts.summary: node-redis is the officially maintained client and the one Redis now recommends for new projects, with TypeScript types and support for new commands. ioredis remains widely used in existing code. Pick one per codebase and learn its argument style.
concepts.production: A migration from ioredis to node-redis needed attention to option syntax such as {{set(key, value, {EX: 10})}}.
concepts.interview: State which you would pick for a new service and why.

concepts.title: Connection lifecycle and the error handler
concepts.summary: Create one client per process, call {{connect()}} explicitly in node-redis and always attach an {{error}} listener. Without a listener, an error is thrown and the process exits.
concepts.production: A missing error handler crashed every pod when Redis restarted.
concepts.interview: Show the three lines every Redis client setup needs.

concepts.title: Timeouts, retries and failing open
concepts.summary: Set connect and command timeouts, use a reconnect strategy with backoff and jitter, and decide per call whether a Redis failure should fall back to the database (fail open) or reject the request. For a cache, fail open with a circuit breaker.
concepts.production: A hung Redis made every request wait 30 seconds until a 100 ms command timeout and fail-open fallback were added.
concepts.interview: Say what your service does when Redis is down.

concepts.title: Pipelining and transactions
concepts.summary: Pipelines batch commands to save round trips but are not atomic. {{MULTI}}/{{EXEC}} queues commands to run together without interleaving, but there is no rollback of logic errors. {{WATCH}} gives optimistic locking.
concepts.production: A batch of 500 cache writes dropped from 200 ms to 6 ms when pipelined.
concepts.interview: Contrast pipeline, MULTI and Lua.

concepts.title: Lua scripts for atomic logic
concepts.summary: A Lua script runs atomically on the server, ideal for compare-and-delete locks, rate limiters and conditional updates. Keep scripts short, pass keys as KEYS for Cluster, and never block in them.
concepts.production: A safe unlock used a three-line script that deletes only if the token matches.
concepts.interview: Explain why check-then-delete in app code is a race.

concepts.title: Pub/sub and blocking commands need their own connections
concepts.summary: A connection in subscriber mode cannot run normal commands, and blocking commands such as {{BLPOP}} hold a connection. Use dedicated duplicate connections for them so they do not stall your main client.
concepts.production: A blocking pop on the shared client froze all cache reads behind it.
concepts.interview: Say why you duplicate the client for subscribers.

concepts.title: Graceful shutdown with Redis
concepts.summary: On shutdown stop accepting requests, finish in-flight work, then call {{quit()}} so pending replies flush. Closing abruptly can lose queued commands and leave locks to expire on their own.
concepts.production: Pods ended mid-write and left locks held until their TTL expired.
concepts.interview: Describe the order: stop traffic, drain, close Redis, exit.

concepts.title: Serialisation pitfalls in Node
concepts.summary: Strings and Buffers are the wire types. Parse JSON defensively, handle Dates and BigInts explicitly, and keep a schema version in cached objects so new deployments can reject old shapes.
concepts.production: A new release read an old cached shape and crashed until values carried a version field.
concepts.interview: Explain how you roll out a changed cached format.

concepts.title: Key metrics from INFO
concepts.summary: Watch hit ratio ({{keyspace_hits}} and {{keyspace_misses}}), {{evicted_keys}}, {{used_memory}}, connected clients, ops per second, latency and replication lag. Hit ratio alone hides problems, so read it with evictions and latency.
concepts.production: A falling hit ratio and rising evictions were the first signs a release had bloated values.
concepts.interview: List the five metrics on your Redis dashboard.

concepts.title: SCAN, not KEYS; UNLINK, not DEL
concepts.summary: {{KEYS}} walks the whole keyspace in one blocking call. {{SCAN}} iterates in small steps. {{DEL}} on a big key blocks while freeing memory; {{UNLINK}} frees it in the background.
concepts.production: Replacing {{KEYS user:*}} with {{SCAN}} removed periodic multi-second stalls.
concepts.interview: Say when {{SCAN}} can return duplicates.

concepts.title: Slowlog and latency monitoring
concepts.summary: {{SLOWLOG}} records commands over a threshold and {{LATENCY}} tools show spikes. Use them to find big keys, O(N) commands and fork or disk effects. Avoid {{MONITOR}} on busy production instances because it adds heavy overhead.
concepts.production: Slowlog revealed a nightly {{SMEMBERS}} on a million-member set.
concepts.interview: Name two causes of periodic latency spikes.

concepts.title: Finding big and cold keys
concepts.summary: Use {{redis-cli --bigkeys}} or {{--memkeys}} (they scan, so run them carefully), {{MEMORY USAGE}} for individual keys and {{OBJECT FREQ}} or {{OBJECT IDLETIME}} to see usage under LFU or LRU.
concepts.production: A single 300 MB key explained a memory jump traced with a bigkeys scan on a replica.
concepts.interview: Say why you run scans on a replica.

concepts.title: Fragmentation and fork latency
concepts.summary: {{mem_fragmentation_ratio}} well above 1 means memory is held but not used; active defragmentation can help. Snapshots fork the process, and copy-on-write can spike memory and latency, so leave headroom beyond {{maxmemory}}.
concepts.production: An instance with maxmemory near total RAM was killed by the OS during a snapshot.
concepts.interview: Explain why maxmemory should be below physical memory.

concepts.title: Capacity planning
concepts.summary: Plan for the working set, value growth, replication buffers and snapshot headroom. Load test with realistic key sizes and access skew, and alert at 70 to 80 percent memory.
concepts.production: A load test with uniform keys looked fine while real skewed traffic created a hot shard.
concepts.interview: State how you estimate memory for N keys.

concepts.title: Alerting that matters
concepts.summary: Alert on user impact and capacity: hit ratio drops, eviction spikes, replication lag, rejected connections, latency percentiles and failover events. Each alert should have a runbook.
concepts.production: An eviction-rate alert warned of a bad deploy before database latency moved.
concepts.interview: Describe an actionable cache alert.

concepts.title: Authentication, ACLs and TLS
concepts.summary: Require authentication, use ACLs to give each application its own user limited to the commands and key patterns it needs, and enable TLS in transit. Do not share the default user between services.
concepts.production: A reporting job's credentials could only read its own key prefix.
concepts.interview: Explain least privilege for a Redis user.

concepts.title: Never expose Redis to the internet
concepts.summary: Keep Redis on private networks behind security groups or firewalls. Public instances without protection are scanned and compromised within minutes.
concepts.production: An open port on a test instance was found and wiped by automated scanners.
concepts.interview: State the first three hardening steps.

concepts.title: Dangerous commands
concepts.summary: Restrict or disable commands such as {{FLUSHALL}}, {{FLUSHDB}}, {{CONFIG}}, {{DEBUG}} and {{KEYS}} for application users. ACL categories make this manageable.
concepts.production: A script run against production by mistake called {{FLUSHALL}}; an ACL would have blocked it.
concepts.interview: Show how you stop an app from flushing the cache.

concepts.title: Sensitive data in caches
concepts.summary: Cached data is a copy of your data. Avoid caching secrets and regulated data, set short TTLs, encrypt at rest where required and make sure deletion requests also remove cached copies.
concepts.production: A privacy deletion request missed cached profile copies for a week.
concepts.interview: Say how deletion requests reach the cache.

concepts.title: Tenant isolation and key safety
concepts.summary: Include the tenant in every key and restrict ACL users by key pattern. Never construct keys from raw user input, to prevent key collisions and cross-tenant reads.
concepts.production: A missing tenant prefix let one customer read another's cached report.
concepts.interview: Describe two layers that prevent cross-tenant reads.

concepts.title: Design: a read-heavy product catalogue
concepts.summary: Cache-aside with jittered TTLs, event invalidation on product updates, an in-process L1 for hot items, negative caching for unknown ids and a stale-while-revalidate path for expensive listings. Measure hit ratio and p99.
concepts.production: A catalogue serving 20,000 reads a second used a 99 percent hit ratio so the database saw about 200 reads a second.
concepts.interview: Walk through read, write and failure paths in that order.

concepts.title: Design: a session and token store
concepts.summary: Store sessions with an idle TTL and sliding expiry, replicate for availability, persist if loss is painful, keep payloads small and rotate identifiers. Treat the store as critical, not as a disposable cache.
concepts.production: A session store with replication survived a primary failure with only a brief login prompt for some users.
concepts.interview: Say what data you refuse to keep only in memory.

concepts.title: Design: a feed or timeline cache
concepts.summary: Cache per-user timelines as sorted sets of ids scored by time, fan out on write for most users, fan out on read for celebrities, and trim lists to a bounded length. Hydrate ids into objects through batched reads.
concepts.production: Bounded 800-item timelines kept memory predictable while most opens were served from cache.
concepts.interview: Explain fan-out on write versus on read and the celebrity problem.

concepts.title: Design: an HTTP response cache
concepts.summary: Layer caches: CDN for public data, Redis for shared computed results, in-process for tiny hot values. Key by every varying input, respect {{Cache-Control}} and decide who invalidates which layer.
concepts.production: A report endpoint cached computed JSON in Redis for 30 seconds and absorbed a traffic spike.
concepts.interview: Say which layer you would hit first and why.

concepts.title: Design: a global leaderboard
concepts.summary: A sorted set holds scores, {{ZINCRBY}} updates them and range commands read ranks. Shard by period or region for scale, and snapshot to a database for history.
concepts.production: Weekly leaderboards used one sorted set per week and expired the old ones.
concepts.interview: State the cost of getting one player's rank.

concepts.title: Design: a distributed rate limiter
concepts.summary: Use a token bucket or sliding window per key held in Redis through a Lua script, return 429 with {{Retry-After}}, and decide fail-open or fail-closed when Redis is unavailable. Add local pre-limits to shave Redis load.
concepts.production: A limiter protecting a login endpoint failed closed for logins but open for read APIs.
concepts.interview: Justify your fail-open or fail-closed choice per endpoint.

questions.q: Why add a cache, and how do you know it helps?
questions.a: A cache lowers latency and origin load. Measure hit ratio, p99 latency and database load before and after. Origin load equals traffic times miss ratio, so raising hits from 95 to 99 percent cuts load five-fold. A cache with a low hit ratio just adds cost.

questions.q: Why is Redis fast, and what is the catch?
questions.a: Data is in memory and commands run on one thread with efficient structures, so each command is atomic and quick. The catch is that one slow O(N) command or huge key blocks every client.

questions.q: What happens if your entire Redis cache is lost?
questions.a: The system must continue from the database, only slower. Protect the origin with rate limits, single-flight rebuilds and gradual warm-up. If losing the cache loses data, Redis is being used as a primary store and needs persistence and replication.

questions.q: Redis or Valkey?
questions.a: Valkey is a BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2 backed by the Linux Foundation and supported by major clouds. Redis 8 is available under a choice of licences including AGPLv3 and bundles more modules. Core commands are compatible, so decide on licensing, managed-service support and the features you need.

questions.q: Describe cache-aside.
questions.a: On a read, check the cache, then the database on a miss, then store the result with a TTL. On a write, update the database and delete the key. The cache is optional, so failures only cost latency.

questions.q: Cache-aside versus read-through?
questions.a: In cache-aside the application owns the load logic. In read-through the cache layer loads from the database through a configured loader, centralising TTL and stampede handling but making the layer critical. Redis needs a library or wrapper for read-through.

questions.q: When would you pick write-through?
questions.a: When data is read soon after being written and consistency matters, such as reference data. Writes are slower because they wait for both cache and database, and unread data fills memory.

questions.q: What are the risks of write-behind?
questions.a: Data loss if the cache fails before flushing, harder ordering and retries, and complex reconciliation. Use a durable queue or stream, accept loss only for approximate data such as counters, and monitor the backlog.

questions.q: When is write-around useful?
questions.a: For write-heavy, rarely read data such as logs or events, so writes do not pollute the cache. The first read misses, which is fine for that profile.

questions.q: Explain stale-while-revalidate and refresh-ahead.
questions.a: Serve a value past its soft TTL while one background call refreshes it, or refresh hot entries before expiry. Users avoid reload latency and stampedes, at the cost of bounded staleness and extra complexity.

questions.q: How do you design a two-level cache?
questions.a: A small in-process L1 with a short TTL for the hottest keys, and Redis as shared L2. Keep L1 fresh with short TTLs and invalidation messages over pub/sub or a stream. It removes hot-key pressure and network latency.

questions.q: How do you pick a TTL?
questions.a: From the business tolerance for stale data, per data type. Stable descriptions can live for hours; stock levels for seconds. Always set a TTL on cache keys so orphaned entries disappear.

questions.q: Why add jitter to TTLs?
questions.a: Keys written together expire together, causing synchronised misses and database spikes. Randomising TTLs by around 10 to 20 percent spreads rebuilds over time.

questions.q: Which eviction policy for a cache, and why not noeviction?
questions.a: Use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu so Redis frees space automatically. With noeviction, writes fail with OOM errors once memory is full. Use volatile policies only when some keys must never be evicted.

questions.q: LRU or LFU?
questions.a: LRU evicts the least recently used key and can be flushed by a scan of one-off keys. LFU evicts the least frequently used and protects popular keys from scans. Redis approximates both by sampling.

questions.q: Why does memory not drop at the exact TTL?
questions.a: Expiry is lazy (on access) and active (periodic sampling), so expired keys can linger briefly. Large numbers expiring together can also add CPU work.

questions.q: Why delete the cache entry instead of updating it after a write?
questions.a: Updating means two writers can set the cache in the opposite order of their database commits, leaving a stale value. Deleting lets the next read rebuild from the source of truth.

questions.q: Explain the cache-aside race condition.
questions.a: A reader misses and loads the old row. A writer updates the database and deletes the key. The reader then stores its old value. The cache stays stale until TTL. Mitigate with short TTLs, versioned values, a delayed second delete or invalidation from a change stream.

questions.q: How do you invalidate from events reliably?
questions.a: Publish changes through an outbox or change data capture and have consumers delete or refresh keys. Use a durable stream, not plain pub/sub, for important invalidations, and keep TTLs as a safety net.

questions.q: What are versioned keys?
questions.a: Keys include a version such as catalog:v7:item:42. Bumping the version invalidates the whole group at once without deleting keys. Old keys expire or are evicted naturally.

questions.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: When a popular key expires, many requests rebuild it at once and overload the origin. Prevent with single-flight or locks, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate and probabilistic early refresh.

questions.q: Stampede, avalanche and penetration: what is the difference?
questions.a: Stampede: one hot key expires and many requests rebuild it. Avalanche: many keys expire together or the cache fails. Penetration: requests for nonexistent keys always reach the database.

questions.q: How do you stop cache penetration?
questions.a: Cache misses for a short TTL, validate ids, rate limit abusive clients and put a Bloom filter in front for very large id spaces.

questions.q: How do you fix a hot key?
questions.a: Serve it from an in-process L1 cache with a short TTL, replicate it under several suffixed keys, use read replicas or split counters. Adding shards does not help because one key lives on one node.

questions.q: Why are big keys a problem?
questions.a: They make reads and deletes slow, block the single thread and unbalance memory. Split them, page collections and use UNLINK for asynchronous deletion.

questions.q: How can a cache leak data between users?
questions.a: If the key omits an input that changes the response (user, tenant, locale), one request can receive another's cached result. Include every varying dimension and never cache per-user data under shared keys.

questions.q: How do you name keys?
questions.a: Use a consistent hierarchical scheme such as service:entity:id:variant, include a version where formats change and never build keys from raw user input.

questions.q: String, hash or JSON for an object?
questions.a: A string suits opaque blobs. A hash suits objects where you read or update fields independently and is memory-efficient when small. JSON documents allow path queries but cost more memory.

questions.q: How do you implement a leaderboard?
questions.a: Use a sorted set with ZADD or ZINCRBY for scores, ZREVRANGE for the top N and ZREVRANK for a player's position. Operations are O(log N). Expire old periods and snapshot to a database for history.

questions.q: How do you count unique visitors at scale?
questions.a: Use HyperLogLog for approximate unique counts in about 12 KB with roughly 1 percent error, or a set when you need exact counts and can afford the memory.

questions.q: Why can many small keys waste memory?
questions.a: Each key has fixed overhead beyond its value. Group small related values into hashes and measure with MEMORY USAGE instead of guessing.

questions.q: Design a rate limiter with Redis.
questions.a: Use INCR with an expiry for fixed windows, a sorted set for sliding windows or a Lua token bucket for bursts, all keyed by user or API key. Return 429 with Retry-After and choose fail-open or fail-closed if Redis is unavailable.

questions.q: Can you trust a Redis distributed lock?
questions.a: Only as an efficiency tool. SET NX PX with a unique token and a compare-and-delete release works in normal cases, but TTL expiry during pauses or failover can allow two holders. Use fencing tokens or database constraints for correctness.

questions.q: Pub/sub, lists or streams for messaging?
questions.a: Pub/sub is fire and forget with no replay. Lists give simple queues. Streams provide durable logs with consumer groups and acknowledgements. Use streams or BullMQ when you cannot lose messages.

questions.q: Where should sessions live?
questions.a: Redis is a good fit: fast, TTL-based and shared across instances. Replicate and persist if losing sessions is costly, and keep them small.

questions.q: Sentinel or Cluster?
questions.a: Sentinel provides failover for a single primary dataset. Cluster shards data across many primaries by hash slot and also fails over. Choose Cluster when data or throughput exceeds one node.

questions.q: How do hash slots and hash tags work?
questions.a: Redis Cluster maps each key to one of 16,384 slots using CRC16 of the key. A hash tag in braces, such as {user:1}:cart, makes only the tag count, so related keys share a slot and multi-key commands work.

questions.q: Why do multi-key operations fail in Cluster?
questions.a: They require all keys to be in the same slot, otherwise the server returns a CROSSSLOT error. Design key tags up front and avoid cross-entity transactions.

questions.q: RDB or AOF?
questions.a: RDB takes periodic snapshots: compact, fast restart, but a larger loss window. AOF logs each write and can fsync every second: smaller loss window, bigger files. Many deployments use both. Snapshots fork the process and can add latency.

questions.q: What can you lose during a failover?
questions.a: Writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated. Replication is asynchronous, so classify data as rebuildable, approximate or critical, and use WAIT or a durable store where needed.

questions.q: What must every Node.js Redis client setup include?
questions.a: One shared client per process, an explicit connect where required, an error event listener (otherwise errors can crash the process), timeouts and a reconnect strategy with backoff.

questions.q: What should happen when Redis is down?
questions.a: For a cache, fail open: short timeouts, fall back to the database and use a circuit breaker so you do not spend time on a dead connection. Protect the database with rate limits and single-flight.

questions.q: Pipeline, MULTI or Lua?
questions.a: A pipeline batches commands to save round trips but is not atomic. MULTI/EXEC runs queued commands without interleaving. Lua runs logic atomically on the server, including conditionals.

questions.q: Why use separate connections for subscribers and blocking commands?
questions.a: A connection in subscribe mode cannot run normal commands, and blocking commands hold the connection. Duplicate the client so they do not stall regular traffic.

questions.q: Which Redis metrics matter for a cache?
questions.a: Hit ratio (keyspace hits and misses), evicted keys, memory used against maxmemory, latency, connected clients, ops per second and replication lag.

questions.q: Why avoid KEYS and DEL on large data?
questions.a: KEYS walks the whole keyspace in one blocking call. DEL on a huge key blocks while freeing memory. Use SCAN for iteration and UNLINK for background deletion.

questions.q: How do you find the cause of periodic latency spikes?
questions.a: Check SLOWLOG and latency monitoring, match spikes to cron jobs, scan for big keys on a replica, and look for fork latency during snapshots.

questions.q: Why should maxmemory be below physical RAM?
questions.a: Snapshots fork the process and copy-on-write can raise memory use, and buffers and fragmentation add overhead. Without headroom the OS can kill Redis.

questions.q: How do you secure Redis?
questions.a: Keep it on a private network, require authentication, use ACL users with least privilege, enable TLS, and restrict dangerous commands such as FLUSHALL, CONFIG and DEBUG.

questions.q: How do you isolate tenants in a shared Redis?
questions.a: Include the tenant in every key, restrict ACL users to key patterns, and never build keys from raw input. For strong isolation use separate instances.

questions.q: Design a cache for a read-heavy product catalogue.
questions.a: Cache-aside with jittered TTLs, event-driven invalidation on updates, an in-process L1 for the hottest items, negative caching and stale-while-revalidate for expensive listings. Track hit ratio and p99, and make sure the database survives a cold cache.

questions.q: Design a timeline cache for a social feed.
questions.a: Store each user's timeline as a bounded sorted set of ids scored by time. Fan out on write for most users and on read for accounts with huge followings, then hydrate ids with batched reads.

questions.q: How would you roll out a changed cached object format?
questions.a: Version the key or the value, deploy readers that accept both, switch writers, then retire the old format. Old entries age out through TTL.

questions.q: Cache keys per tenant, locale and API version: how?
questions.a: Include every input that changes the response in the key, for example tenant:locale:v2:resource:id. A missing dimension causes data leaks.

drills.title: Database CPU spikes every hour on the hour
drills.context: A product API shows database CPU jumping to 100 percent for about 20 seconds at the top of every hour. The cache hit ratio falls to near zero at the same moment and then recovers.
symptoms: Spikes line up exactly with the clock
Hit ratio drops then recovers by itself
The slow queries are the same few hundred repeated

options.why: GC pauses are not scheduled to the hour and do not empty the cache.

options.text: Keys with the same TTL expire together (a stampede)
options.why: A bulk warm-up wrote keys with an identical 1 hour TTL, so they all expire and rebuild at once.
Redis would report errors and failovers, not a clean recovery in seconds.
DNS would not produce identical repeated database queries.

path: Plot hit ratio and database queries per second against time
Sample TTL values of hot keys: are they identical or clustered?
Find the job that wrote the keys together, such as a warm-up
drills.fix: Add jitter to TTLs, rebuild with single-flight so one request reloads each key, and serve stale while revalidating for the hottest keys.
drills.prevent: Alert on hit ratio drops, load test cold-cache behaviour and review every bulk write for TTL spread.
drills.interview: Name three defences: jitter, single-flight, stale-while-revalidate.

drills.title: Users see old prices after an update
drills.context: An admin changes a product price. The database has the new value immediately, but some users still see the old price for several minutes. The write path deletes the cache key after committing.
symptoms: Only some users are affected
The staleness lasts about as long as the TTL
Writes always delete the key after commit

options.text: A slow reader repopulated the cache with the old value after the delete
options.why: The reader loaded the old row before the commit and stored it after the delete, so the stale value stayed until the TTL.
Lag lasts milliseconds, not minutes, and the writer deleted the key.
A failed delete would affect everyone, not some users.
A short TTL would reduce staleness, not cause it.

path: Reconstruct the interleaving of read, commit and delete from timestamps
Check whether the stored value carries a version or timestamp
Confirm the TTL is the only thing that eventually heals it
drills.fix: Shorten the TTL for volatile data, store a version and refuse older writes, use a delayed second delete, or invalidate from a change stream after commit.
drills.prevent: Treat the cache-aside race as expected, keep TTLs as a safety net and test concurrent read and write paths.
drills.interview: Draw the three-step interleaving on the whiteboard before proposing a fix.

drills.title: Latency spikes every five minutes
drills.context: p99 latency for every service using the shared Redis jumps from 2 ms to 800 ms for about a second, every five minutes. CPU on the Redis host looks low overall.
symptoms: All clients are affected at the same instant
Spikes repeat on a schedule
Average CPU is low but one core is busy

options.why: Packet loss would not be perfectly periodic and would not affect every client together.

options.text: A slow O(N) command or big key blocks the single thread
options.why: A scheduled job running a large SMEMBERS or deleting a huge key blocks all other commands.
A small pool would hurt individual services, not all clients at one instant.
Eviction changes hit ratio, not periodic one-second freezes.

path: Check SLOWLOG for commands over the threshold at those times
Match the timing to cron jobs or batch tasks
Inspect for big keys with a scan on a replica
drills.fix: Replace the O(N) command with SCAN or paging, split the big key, use UNLINK for deletes and move the batch to a replica or off-peak.
drills.prevent: Alert on slowlog entries, set key size limits and code-review commands used in batch jobs.
drills.interview: Explain why a single-threaded executor makes one slow command everyone's problem.

drills.title: Writes fail with OOM errors
drills.context: During a traffic peak the application begins logging "OOM command not allowed when used memory is greater than maxmemory". Reads still work but cache writes fail and the hit ratio decays.
symptoms: Memory is at the configured maximum
Errors appear only on write commands
The instance is used as a cache

options.why: With noeviction Redis refuses writes at the limit instead of evicting old keys.
The errors come from the Redis server, not the application process.
Connection limits produce different errors.
A client version would not produce a server OOM message.

path: Read maxmemory and maxmemory-policy with CONFIG GET
Compare used_memory with maxmemory and check evicted_keys
Look for recent value size growth or missing TTLs
drills.fix: Use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for pure caches, set TTLs on every cache key and increase memory if the working set no longer fits.
drills.prevent: Alert at 75 percent memory, load test value growth and separate queues or sessions from the cache instance.
drills.interview: Say which policy you use for a cache and which for a session store.

drills.title: Database overloaded by lookups for ids that do not exist
drills.context: Database load climbs steadily and a few queries dominate, all lookups by id that return no rows. The cache hit ratio for that endpoint is close to zero.
symptoms: Queries return empty results
Ids look random or sequential beyond the real range
Cache hit ratio is near zero for that route

options.why: Misses are never cached, so every request for a missing id reaches the database.
A stampede involves one existing hot key, not many nonexistent ones.
A disk problem would not target missing ids.
Lag does not create empty lookups.

path: Group slow queries by result: are they all empty?
Inspect request logs for patterns of ids or a single client
Check whether misses are cached at all
drills.fix: Cache misses for a short TTL, validate id format and range, rate limit the source and consider a Bloom filter in front for very large id spaces.
drills.prevent: Track miss ratio per endpoint and alert on a sudden rise.
drills.interview: Explain why the negative TTL must be short.

drills.title: One cluster node at 100 percent CPU
drills.context: In a six-shard Redis Cluster, one primary is saturated while the others sit near 10 percent. Adding shards did not help.
symptoms: Load is uneven across shards
A single key appears in most slowlog entries
More shards changed nothing

options.text: A hot key concentrated on one shard
options.why: One key maps to one slot on one node, so adding nodes cannot spread its traffic.
Replica count does not explain one primary at full CPU.
Gossip cost is small and spread across nodes.
Drift would not concentrate CPU on one node.

path: Use redis-cli --hotkeys (with LFU) or sample commands to find the hottest key
Check which slot and node serve it
Estimate its request rate
drills.fix: Serve the key from an in-process L1 cache with a short TTL, replicate it under several suffixed keys for reads, or split counters across keys.
drills.prevent: Load test with realistic skew and watch per-shard CPU, not only cluster averages.
drills.interview: Say why adding shards cannot fix a single hot key.

drills.title: Two workers ran the same job despite a lock
drills.context: A billing job takes a Redis lock with a 30 second TTL. Occasionally two workers run it at the same time and customers are billed twice. The lock code is correct and uses SET NX PX.
symptoms: Duplicates are rare
The job sometimes takes longer than 30 seconds
Both workers believed they held the lock

options.text: The lock TTL expired while the first worker was still running
options.why: A slow job or GC pause outlived the TTL, the lock expired and a second worker took it.
It is possible after failover but does not explain the correlation with long jobs.
SET with NX and PX is atomic.
That would fail every time, not occasionally.

path: Compare job duration with the lock TTL in the logs
Look for GC pauses or slow dependencies in the first worker
Check whether the job is idempotent
drills.fix: Make the job idempotent with a database constraint, use fencing tokens, renew the lock while working and keep the lock as an efficiency tool rather than a correctness guarantee.
drills.prevent: Alert when jobs exceed their lock TTL and test lock expiry in the middle of work.
drills.interview: State that Redis locks are best effort and that correctness belongs in the database.

drills.title: Counters go missing after a failover
drills.context: After a primary failed and a replica was promoted, the last few seconds of view counters were missing. Nothing was wrong with the application code.
symptoms: Missing data covers only the seconds before the failover
Everything older is intact
The cluster used default replication

options.text: Asynchronous replication lost writes not yet copied
options.why: The old primary acknowledged writes that had not reached the replica before it failed.
A bug would not align with the failover moment.
Counters older than that window were intact.
Eviction would not target the most recent seconds.

path: Check replication offset and lag at failure time
Confirm the failover time against the missing window
Review how persistence and acknowledgement are configured
drills.fix: Accept the small loss for approximate counters, or write important counts to a durable store and reconcile. Use WAIT for stronger acknowledgement where it matters.
drills.prevent: Document the data-loss window and classify each use of Redis as rebuildable, approximate or critical.
drills.interview: Describe exactly what Redis replication does and does not promise.

incidents.title: Facebook outage, September 2010
incidents.body: An invalid configuration value stored in a cache was detected as bad by every client, and each client tried to fix it by querying the database. The query load overwhelmed the database in a feedback loop and took the site down for hours. Lesson: protect the origin from client-driven retry storms.

incidents.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook, 2013
incidents.body: The paper describes leases that stop a stampede and prevent stale sets, along with regional pools and cold-cluster warm-up. Worth reading for the origin of many patterns used with Redis today.

incidents.title: Optimal probabilistic cache stampede prevention, 2015
incidents.body: Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein describe XFetch: each request may refresh a key early with a probability that rises as expiry nears, avoiding locks. Lesson: stampedes can be prevented without coordination.

incidents.title: Redis licence changes and Valkey, 2024 to 2025
incidents.body: Redis moved away from its permissive licence, the community and cloud vendors created Valkey, and Redis 8 later added AGPLv3 as an option. Lesson: know your dependency's licence, governance and compatibility before standardising.

codeLab.title: Cache-aside helper with jitter and negative caching
codeLab.brief: Fail open on Redis errors, cache misses briefly and spread TTLs.

codeLab.title: Stampede protection: single-flight plus a Redis lock
codeLab.brief: Only one request per process, and ideally one per cluster, rebuilds a key.

codeLab.title: Stale-while-revalidate with a soft TTL
codeLab.brief: Serve a slightly old value while refreshing in the background.

codeLab.title: Atomic fixed-window rate limiter with Lua
codeLab.brief: INCR and EXPIRE in one atomic step so a crash cannot leave a counter with no expiry.

codeLab.title: Safe distributed lock
codeLab.brief: Acquire with SET NX PX and release only if the token still matches.

codeLab.title: Versioned keys for group invalidation
codeLab.brief: Bump a version counter instead of deleting thousands of keys.

codeLab.title: Two-level cache with pub/sub invalidation
codeLab.brief: In-process L1 for hot reads, Redis L2, and messages to clear L1 across pods.

codeLab.title: Delete by pattern with SCAN and UNLINK
codeLab.brief: Never use KEYS in production. In Cluster, scan each primary separately.

codeLab.title: Leaderboard with sorted sets
codeLab.brief: Increment scores, read the top N and find one player's rank.

items.name: Cache-aside
items.description: The application owns the logic: look in the cache, fall back to the database on a miss and fill the cache. On writes it updates the database and deletes the key.

write.action: DEL the key (do not update it)
Misses and repopulates from the database

items.useWhen: Read-heavy data where slight staleness is fine, and where the cache may fail without breaking correctness. It is the default choice.
items.watchOut: The read and write race can store stale values until the TTL. Cold keys cause a miss penalty and stampedes on hot keys.

items.name: Read-through
items.description: The caller only talks to the cache layer. On a miss, the layer itself calls a loader function to fetch from the database. Redis does not do this natively; a library or wrapper provides it.

read.action: On a miss, run the loader

write.action: Writes usually go to the database (or use write-through)

items.useWhen: You want one consistent loading, TTL and stampede policy shared by many callers.
items.watchOut: The cache layer becomes critical infrastructure. If it fails, the app cannot read at all unless it can bypass it.

items.name: Write-through
items.description: Writes go through the cache and synchronously to the database. The write returns only when both have succeeded, so reads always find fresh data.
items.useWhen: Data read soon after it is written, such as reference data, where consistency matters more than write latency.
items.watchOut: Slower writes, and the cache fills with data that may never be read. A failure between the two writes needs handling.

items.name: Write-behind
items.description: Writes are acknowledged once they reach the cache. A background process flushes them to the database later, often in batches.

write.action: Write the value and acknowledge quickly
Hold the change durably (stream or queue)

items.useWhen: Very high write rates where small data loss is acceptable, such as counters, metrics or view counts.
items.watchOut: A crash before the flush loses data. Ordering and failure handling are complex. Never use it for money without a durable queue.

items.name: Write-around
items.description: Writes skip the cache and go straight to the database. Reads use cache-aside, so data enters the cache only when it is read.

read.action: On a miss, query the row

write.action: Not touched (rely on TTL or a delete)

items.useWhen: Write-heavy data that is rarely read back, such as logs or events, so the cache is not polluted.
items.watchOut: The first read after a write is a miss, and cached copies can be stale unless you invalidate.

items.name: Refresh-ahead
items.description: Hot keys are refreshed before they expire, or a stale value is served while one background call refreshes it, so users rarely wait for a reload.
items.useWhen: A small set of expensive, hot keys where reload latency or stampedes are unacceptable.
items.watchOut: Extra complexity, wasted refreshes for keys nobody reads again, and slightly stale data.

frameworks.name: The six-question cache design framework
steps: What am I caching, and what hit ratio do I need to hit my latency and load targets?
Which pattern fits the read and write mix and the staleness budget?
How long does an entry live, and how is it invalidated when data changes?
What happens on a miss storm, a cold start or a Redis outage?
How do I size memory and choose eviction for the working set?
How will I observe hit ratio, evictions, latency and staleness?

frameworks.name: The trade-off sentence
steps: I would use cache-aside because reads dominate and slight staleness is acceptable.
The cost is a possible stale window after writes, which I would bound with a short TTL and delete-on-write.
If freshness requirements tighten, I would add event-driven invalidation or move that data to write-through.

frameworks.name: Answering "what if Redis goes down?"
steps: State that the database must survive a cold cache, or the design is wrong.
Fail open with timeouts and a circuit breaker.
Protect the origin with rate limits, single-flight and load shedding.
Warm the cache gradually after recovery.

frameworks.name: Debugging a cache problem
steps: Observe: hit ratio, evictions, latency, database load.
Hypothesise: stampede, penetration, hot key, big key, eviction, race.
Test: slowlog, key samples, TTL distribution, timelines.
Fix, then prevent with an alert and a load test.

glance.title: Hit-ratio maths
glance.text: Origin load = traffic times miss ratio. 95 to 99 percent hits is five-fold less load.

glance.title: Cache-aside
glance.text: Read cache, then database, then fill. On write, update the database and delete the key.

glance.title: Delete, do not update
glance.text: Updating the cache races with other writers. Deleting lets the next read rebuild.

glance.title: Stampede defence
glance.text: Jitter TTLs, single-flight or lock, stale-while-revalidate, probabilistic early refresh.

glance.title: Penetration defence
glance.text: Cache misses briefly, validate ids, rate limit, Bloom filter for huge id spaces.

glance.title: Eviction choice
glance.text: Cache: allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu. Never noeviction for a cache.

glance.title: Single thread
glance.text: Commands are atomic but a slow O(N) command blocks everyone. Use SCAN and UNLINK.

glance.title: Replication is async
glance.text: Failover can lose recent writes. Replicas can serve stale reads.

glance.title: Cluster slots
glance.text: 16,384 slots by CRC16. Hash tags group keys. Multi-key operations need one slot.

glance.title: Locks are best effort
glance.text: SET NX PX with a token and Lua unlock. Use fencing or database constraints for correctness.

glance.title: Hot and big keys
glance.text: Hot: L1 cache or key splitting. Big: split, page and UNLINK.

glance.title: Cache is never the source of truth
glance.text: The system must survive an empty cache. Classify data as rebuildable, approximate or critical.

lists.title: Questions to ask the interviewer
items: What is your cache hit ratio and how do you track it?
How do you invalidate caches when data changes?
Have you had a stampede or cold-cache incident?
Which Redis or Valkey version and hosting do you use?
Who owns cache keys and TTL decisions?
How do you test the system with an empty cache?

lists.title: Red flags in answers
items: Caching everything without measuring
Updating the cache and database in two unsynchronised steps
No TTL on cache keys
Treating Redis as a durable database without discussing persistence
Using KEYS in production
Ignoring what happens when Redis is down

lists.title: Good phrases to use
items: "I would measure the hit ratio before and after."
"The database has to survive a cold cache."
"TTL is the safety net, events give freshness."
"This is rebuildable, so loss is acceptable."
"I would fail open with a timeout and a breaker."
"A hot key cannot be fixed by adding shards."

lists.title: Common whiteboard tasks
items: Draw cache-aside with read and write paths

Design a rate limiter with Redis
Design a leaderboard or feed cache
Explain how a key maps to a cluster slot
Compare cache-aside with write-through and write-behind

stories.title: Cut database load by 80 percent with caching
parts: Situation: a catalogue API sent every read to the database and p99 latency reached 900 ms at peak.
Task: bring latency under 200 ms without stale prices.

Action: I measured read patterns, chose cache-aside with jittered TTLs by data volatility, added event-driven invalidation for prices, in-process caching for the hottest items and hit-ratio and eviction dashboards.
Result: hit ratio reached 97 percent, database reads fell by about 80 percent and p99 dropped to 140 ms.
Learning: measure first, and treat invalidation as part of the design, not an afterthought.

stories.title: Fixed an hourly stampede
parts: Situation: database CPU hit 100 percent every hour and the API timed out for about 20 seconds.
Task: find the cause and stop it recurring.
Action: plotted hit ratio against time, saw identical TTLs from a bulk warm-up, added jitter, single-flight rebuilds and stale-while-revalidate for the hottest keys and an alert on hit-ratio drops.
Result: the hourly spike disappeared and the database peak fell by 70 percent.
Learning: bulk writes need the same scrutiny as application code.
